title: Earth and Environmental Science
description: From the layers of the planet to its energy balance, weather, oceans, carbon cycle and living systems, with the numbers needed to reason about them.
audience: A capable adult with basic maths who has met energy and forces in Discere's physics course and ecosystems in biology. No geology or meteorology assumed.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain how we know the interior of the Earth and calculate plate motion.
You'll be able to classify rocks and date a sample from its half-life.
You'll be able to compute Earth's energy balance and explain the greenhouse effect with numbers.
You'll be able to read weather from pressure, rotation and rising air.
You'll be able to convert carbon units, relate forcing to warming and judge climate evidence.
You'll be able to follow energy through an ecosystem and do stock and flow arithmetic for resources.

modules.title: The solid Earth
modules.summary: Layers, moving plates, the rock cycle and the clock that dates them.

modules.title: Air, energy and water
modules.summary: The atmosphere, the energy it balances, the weather it carries and the oceans that store heat.

modules.title: Climate, life and resources
modules.summary: The carbon cycle, what has changed and why, how ecosystems pass energy along, and the limits on what people draw from them.

lessons.title: What lies beneath
lessons.objective: Describe Earth's layers and explain how seismic waves showed they exist.

concepts.title: Earth's layers
concepts.summary: Crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core, separated by changes in composition and in wave speed.

concepts.title: Seismic evidence
concepts.summary: P waves pass through solids and liquids; S waves pass through solids only, so the S-wave shadow shows a liquid outer core.

misconceptions: The Earth is a thin shell around a sea of magma. The mantle is solid rock that flows over millions of years; only the outer core is liquid.
Layers were seen by drilling. The deepest borehole reaches about 12 km; the layers were found by waves.
The crust is similar everywhere. Oceanic crust is about 7 km thick and basaltic; continental crust averages about 35 km and is lighter.
sequence: Scale first: radius 6,371 km, deepest borehole 12 km.
Introduce earthquake waves as the only way to see inside.
Show P and S waves and the S-wave shadow on the far side.
Place the boundaries by depth and name each layer.
Check understanding with a depth-to-radius calculation.
examples: The core-mantle boundary lies 2,891 km down, so the core radius is 6,371 - 2,891 = 3,480 km.
An earthquake's S waves are missing across an angular band on the far side: a liquid layer stops them.

figures.shows: Cross-section of Earth to scale with switchable views: layers, P-wave paths, S-wave shadow.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a wave type and see where it can travel.

questionPlan.sample: The core-mantle boundary is 2,891 km deep and Earth's radius is 6,371 km. What is the radius of the core, in km?
S waves do not arrive on the far side of Earth. What does this show?
questionPlan.answer: Part of the interior is liquid
choices: Part of the interior is liquid
The core is hotter than the mantle
The waves are too slow to arrive

questionPlan.sample: Which layer is the thinnest: crust, mantle or core?

lessons.title: Plates in motion
lessons.objective: Match the three boundary types to what happens there and calculate how far plates move over geological time.

concepts.title: Plate boundaries
concepts.summary: Divergent plates move apart, convergent plates collide or one sinks (subduction), transform plates slide past each other.

concepts.title: Plate speed
concepts.summary: Plates move at centimetres per year; 1 cm per year is 10 km per million years.

misconceptions: Continents plough through the ocean floor. The seafloor and continents move together as part of plates.
Earthquakes and volcanoes occur everywhere at random. They cluster along boundaries, with the Pacific Ring of Fire the largest.
A rate of centimetres a year is negligible. Over 10 million years it is hundreds of kilometres.
sequence: Begin with the fit of the Atlantic coasts and Wegener's 1912 proposal, and why geologists rejected it: no mechanism.
Seafloor evidence: ridges, young oceanic crust, magnetic stripes symmetric about the ridge.
Three boundary types, each with its landforms.
Hotspots: a fixed source and a moving plate leave an age-progressive chain.
Convert rates to distances.
examples: 2.5 cm/yr for 10 million years: 0.025 m x 10,000,000 = 250 km.
Two volcanic islands 800 km apart whose ages differ by 8 million years mark a plate speed of 800 km / 8 Myr = 100 km/Myr = 10 cm/yr.

figures.shows: Three side-view cross-sections: ridge, subduction trench, transform fault; switchable.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a boundary and see arrows, quakes and volcanoes appear.

figures.shows: Hawaiian-Emperor island chain with ages along the track.
figures.learnerAction: Scrub along the chain and read ages and distances.

questionPlan.sample: A plate moves 4 cm per year. How far does it move in 50 million years, in km?
Two islands in a hotspot chain are 800 km apart and 8 million years apart in age. What is the plate speed in cm per year?
The Himalayas are rising where two continental plates collide. What type of boundary is this?

historyNotes: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and published The Origin of Continents and Oceans in 1915. Plate tectonics was accepted in the 1960s after seafloor spreading and magnetic stripe evidence.

lessons.title: The rock cycle
lessons.objective: Classify a rock by how it formed and trace a path through the rock cycle.

concepts.title: Three rock families
concepts.summary: Igneous rock cools from melt, sedimentary rock builds from deposited grains, metamorphic rock changes in the solid state under heat and pressure.

concepts.title: Crystal size and cooling
concepts.summary: Slow cooling underground makes large crystals; fast cooling at the surface makes small ones or glass.

misconceptions: The cycle is a fixed loop that every rock follows in order. Any rock can go to any other family by several routes.
Metamorphic means melted. It means changed in the solid state; melting makes igneous rock.
Sedimentary layers are deposited quickly. Rates are tiny on average, with long gaps in the record.
sequence: Start with a hand specimen: granite with large crystals versus basalt with small ones.
Link crystal size to cooling history.
Weathering, transport, deposition, burial and cementation make sedimentary rock.
Heat and pressure make metamorphic rock; examples: limestone to marble, shale to slate to gneiss.
Draw the web of arrows, not a ring.
examples: Granite is coarse-grained and formed by slow cooling of magma at depth. Basalt is fine-grained and formed by fast cooling of lava at the surface.
50 m of shale deposited at an average 0.1 mm per year represents 50,000 mm / 0.1 = 500,000 years (illustrative rate).

figures.shows: Four rock photographs or drawings with texture labels hidden; pick the formation process.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the process for each sample.

figures.shows: The rock cycle as a web of arrows between magma, igneous, sediment, sedimentary and metamorphic.
figures.learnerAction: Click a process to highlight its arrow.

questionPlan.sample: A rock is made of large interlocking crystals and has no layers. Which formation story fits best?
choices: Fast cooling of lava at the surface

questionPlan.sample: Granite changes under heat and pressure, without melting, into gneiss. What family is gneiss?
Shale builds up at an average 0.1 mm per year. How many years does 50 m take?

lessons.title: Reading deep time
lessons.objective: Use half-lives to date a sample and scale Earth history onto a clock face.

concepts.title: Half-life
concepts.summary: The time for half the atoms of a radioactive isotope to decay; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n.

concepts.title: Age of Earth
concepts.summary: About 4.54 billion years, from lead isotopes in meteorites and the oldest Earth minerals.

misconceptions: Half-life is read as half the lifetime. After two half-lives a quarter remains, not none.
Radiocarbon dates anything old. Carbon-14 only works to about 50,000 years; older rocks use isotopes with long half-lives such as uranium-238.
Rock layers show a few thousand years. Sedimentary sequences, ice cores and isotopes together show millions and billions.
sequence: Order events by layer: the oldest at the bottom, with cross-cutting relations.
Absolute dates need a clock. Introduce decay.
Compute the fraction left after n half-lives and invert.
Pick the right clock for the age: C-14 5,730 yr, U-238 4.468 billion yr.
Compress 4.54 billion years onto a 24-hour clock.
examples: A sample has 1/8 of its original C-14: three half-lives, 3 x 5,730 = 17,190 years.
On a 24-hour clock, the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago is 66/4,540 of a day before midnight: 66/4540 x 1440 min = 20.9 minutes. Modern humans, about 300,000 years, are about 5.7 seconds.

figures.shows: Earth history on a 24-hour clock with events: oldest minerals, first life, oxygen rise, animals, dinosaurs, humans.
figures.learnerAction: Scrub the clock and read the event times.

figures.shows: Decay curve: fraction remaining against number of half-lives, with points at 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: A bone has 1/8 of its original carbon-14. The half-life is 5,730 years. How old is it, in years?
A rock has one part parent isotope for every three parts daughter. The half-life is 700 million years. How old is it, in billions of years?
Earth is 4,540 million years old, scaled to 24 hours. The dinosaur extinction was 66 million years ago. How many minutes before midnight, to the nearest minute?

historyNotes: Clair Patterson dated meteorites by lead isotopes in 1953 to 1956 and got about 4.55 billion years for the age of Earth.

lessons.title: Layers of air
lessons.objective: State what air is made of and use pressure falling with height.

concepts.title: Atmosphere layers
concepts.summary: Troposphere (weather, falls with height), stratosphere (ozone, rises with height), mesosphere, thermosphere.

concepts.title: Pressure and height
concepts.summary: Air pressure falls roughly by half every 5.5 km near the surface, because pressure is the weight of the air above.

misconceptions: Thin air at altitude has less oxygen by percentage. The mix is the same; the pressure, and so the oxygen pressure, is lower.
Temperature falls steadily up through the atmosphere. It falls through the troposphere, rises in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet, then falls again.
Space starts at a sharp edge. The atmosphere thins gradually.
sequence: Composition: 78.08 percent nitrogen, 20.95 percent oxygen, 0.93 percent argon, about 0.04 percent carbon dioxide, water vapour variable.
Pressure is the weight of the column above.
Halving rule and what it means at Everest and at cruising altitude.
Temperature profile with its four layers and the reason for each turn.
Why almost all weather lives in the troposphere.
examples: Sea-level pressure is 101.3 kPa. At 11 km, two halvings (11/5.5 = 2): 25.3 kPa.
Everest at 8.85 km is about 1.6 halvings: 101.3 / 2^1.61 = 33 kPa, about a third. Oxygen is still 21 percent; its pressure is about 7 kPa.

figures.shows: Two panels: pressure against altitude (exponential fall) and temperature against altitude (zigzag) with layer bands.
figures.learnerAction: Hover an altitude to read pressure and layer.

questionPlan.sample: Sea-level pressure is 101.3 kPa and it halves every 5.5 km. What is the pressure at 11 km, in kPa to one decimal?
At 5.5 km the pressure is 50.65 kPa. Oxygen is 21 percent of the air. What is the pressure of oxygen there, in kPa to one decimal?
In which layer does the ozone layer warm the air?

lessons.title: The energy balance
lessons.objective: Compute absorbed sunlight, the effective temperature and the size of the greenhouse effect.

concepts.title: Albedo
concepts.summary: The fraction of incoming sunlight a surface or planet reflects; Earth's is about 0.30.

concepts.title: Greenhouse effect
concepts.summary: Gases that absorb and re-emit infrared raise the surface temperature above the temperature a bare planet would have.

misconceptions: The greenhouse effect is a fault of pollution. It is natural and keeps the surface at about 15 degrees C rather than about minus 18; added gases strengthen it.
Greenhouse gases trap heat like a glass lid. They absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including down, which changes how energy leaves.
Every square metre receives 1,361 W. Sunlight hits a disc but spreads over a sphere, so the average is a quarter.
sequence: Energy in: sunlight 1,361 W/m2 on a disc facing the sun.
Why divide by 4: disc area pi r^2 against sphere area 4 pi r^2.
Subtract the reflected share (albedo 0.30).
Energy out: Stefan-Boltzmann, emission = sigma T^4 with sigma = 5.67e-8. Balance gives about 255 K.
Observed mean surface temperature is about 288 K; the 33 K difference is the greenhouse effect.
examples: Absorbed = 1361 x (1 - 0.30) / 4 = 238 W/m2. Balanced emission needs T = (238 / 5.67e-8)^0.25 = 255 K, about minus 18 degrees C. Observed 288 K, so the greenhouse effect is about 33 K.
A planet with albedo 0.5 at the same distance absorbs 1361 x 0.5 / 4 = 170 W/m2.

figures.shows: Arrow diagram of Earth: incoming 340, reflected 100, absorbed 240, surface emission, atmosphere absorption and back-radiation; switchable between bare Earth and real Earth.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and compare outgoing arrows.

questionPlan.sample: Sunlight is 1,361 W/m2 and albedo is 0.5. What is the average absorbed power per square metre of the planet's surface, to the nearest W/m2?
A planet emits 240 W/m2. With sigma = 5.67e-8, what temperature in kelvin, to the nearest kelvin, balances this?
Why is the surface warmer than 255 K?
questionPlan.answer: Gases absorb outgoing infrared and radiate part of it back down
choices: The Sun is hotter than the formula assumes
Gases absorb outgoing infrared and radiate part of it back down

lessons.title: Why the weather moves
lessons.objective: Explain wind, fronts and cloud formation from pressure, rotation and rising air.

concepts.title: Pressure gradient
concepts.summary: Air accelerates from high to low pressure; on a rotating Earth it is deflected to the right in the north and to the left in the south.

concepts.title: Cloud base
concepts.summary: Rising air cools about 9.8 degrees C per km until it reaches its dew point; cloud base is about 125 m per degree of gap between temperature and dew point.

misconceptions: Wind blows straight from high to low pressure. The Coriolis deflection makes it nearly parallel to the isobars aloft.
Warm air rises because it is hot, so it keeps warming. Rising air expands and cools.
Weather and climate are the same thing. Weather is the state now; climate is the long-term pattern.
sequence: Uneven heating makes a pressure difference. Show a sea breeze.
Add Earth's rotation: deflection, and the circulation around highs and lows.
Global cells: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies.
Rising air cools and clouds form; fronts lift warm air over cold.
Compute cloud base.
examples: Air at 30 degrees C with dew point 18 degrees C: gap 12 degrees, cloud base about 125 x 12 = 1,500 m.
A parcel at 25 degrees C lifted 1.5 km dry: 25 - 9.8 x 1.5 = 10.3 degrees C.

figures.shows: Map-view low and high with arrows: straight pressure-gradient, then deflected flow; switchable hemispheres.
figures.learnerAction: Switch hemisphere and see the deflection direction.

figures.shows: Temperature and dew point against height for a rising parcel; the lines meet at the cloud base.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Surface temperature is 28 degrees C and dew point 16 degrees C. Using 125 m per degree, what is the cloud base in metres?
In the Northern Hemisphere, which way does air circulate around a low-pressure centre?
Dry air at 25 degrees C is lifted 1.5 km. Using 9.8 degrees per km, what is its temperature in degrees C to one decimal?

lessons.title: The ocean system
lessons.objective: Explain how density drives deep circulation and calculate sea-level change from added water.

concepts.title: Seawater density
concepts.summary: Cold and salty water is denser; dense water sinks and drives the slow global overturning circulation.

concepts.title: Sea-level arithmetic
concepts.summary: Added volume divided by ocean area gives the rise; thermal expansion of warming water adds to it.

misconceptions: Currents are only driven by wind. Wind drives surface currents; density differences drive the deep ones.
Melting sea ice raises sea level. Floating ice displaces its weight of water, so only land ice raises levels.
The ocean is a thin film. It holds most of the heat in the climate system: about 90 percent of the extra heat since 1970 has gone to the ocean.
sequence: Scale: oceans cover 71 percent of the surface, mean depth about 3,700 m, mean salinity about 35 g per kg.
Surface currents from wind and Coriolis: gyres, the Gulf Stream.
Density: cooling and salt in the North Atlantic make water sink; the conveyor.
Heat storage and thermal expansion.
Sea-level arithmetic.
examples: Ocean area is about 361 million km2. Adding 3,610 km3 of water spreads to 3,610 / 361,000,000 = 0.00001 km = 1 cm.
7,220 km3 of meltwater raises the ocean by 20 mm.

figures.shows: Ocean cross-section from pole to equator with sinking water, deep return flow and surface gyres.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between surface and deep layers.

figures.shows: Global mean sea level against year since 1993 from satellite altimetry.
figures.learnerAction: Hover for values.

questionPlan.sample: The ocean area is 361 million km2. How many millimetres does it rise when 7,220 km3 of water is added?
Which water is most likely to sink?
Which melting adds to sea level?
choices: An ice cube in a glass

lessons.title: How carbon moves
lessons.objective: Track carbon between reservoirs and convert between GtC, GtCO2 and ppm.

concepts.title: Carbon reservoirs
concepts.summary: The ocean, soils, vegetation, atmosphere and rocks store carbon; fluxes between them differ greatly in speed.

concepts.title: Carbon units
concepts.summary: 1 GtC equals 44/12 GtCO2, and about 2.13 GtC in the atmosphere raises CO2 by 1 ppm.

misconceptions: Carbon dioxide mass and carbon mass are the same. Carbon is 12/44 of the mass of CO2.
All emissions stay in the air. About 45 percent of fossil emissions remains airborne; land and ocean take up the rest.
The natural carbon cycle swamps human emissions, so ours do not matter. Natural flows roughly balance; ours add on top.
sequence: Reservoirs and rough sizes: atmosphere about 870 GtC today, ocean about 38,000 GtC, soils and plants a few thousand GtC.
Fast cycle (photosynthesis, respiration, ocean exchange) against slow cycle (weathering, burial, volcanism).
Units: GtC to GtCO2 to ppm.
Airborne fraction.
The Keeling curve as the measurement that revealed it: yearly wiggle from plants and the rising trend.
examples: 10 GtC emitted: 10 x 44/12 = 36.7 GtCO2. If 45 percent stays airborne: 4.5 GtC, 4.5 / 2.13 = 2.1 ppm per year.
CO2 rose from about 280 ppm before industry to above 420 ppm, an increase of (420 - 280)/280 = 50 percent.

figures.shows: Monthly CO2 at Mauna Loa from 1958: trend plus seasonal wiggle, with zoom.
figures.learnerAction: Zoom into one year to see the seasonal cycle.

figures.shows: Reservoir boxes with arrows sized by flux, switchable between fast and slow cycle.
figures.learnerAction: Click a reservoir to see its in and out flows.

questionPlan.sample: How many GtCO2 correspond to 12 GtC? Use 44/12.
Emissions are 10 GtC per year, 45 percent stays in the air, and 2.13 GtC raises CO2 by 1 ppm. By how much does CO2 rise in a year, in ppm to one decimal?
CO2 rises from 280 ppm to 420 ppm. What is the percentage increase?

historyNotes: Charles David Keeling began continuous CO2 measurements at Mauna Loa in March 1958 and found the annual rise and seasonal cycle.

lessons.title: What has changed and why
lessons.objective: Relate forcing to warming and weigh the evidence that the recent change is human-driven.

concepts.title: Radiative forcing
concepts.summary: The change in the energy balance from a cause; for CO2, forcing = 5.35 x ln(C / C0) W/m2.

concepts.title: Climate sensitivity
concepts.summary: The equilibrium warming for a doubling of CO2; the IPCC AR6 best estimate is about 3 degrees C with a likely range of 2.5 to 4.

misconceptions: A cold day disproves warming. Weather varies around a trend; climate is a multi-decade average.
Climate changed naturally before, so people cannot be the cause. Past causes (orbits, volcanoes, the Sun) can be measured and do not explain the recent rise.
CO2 is the only driver. Aerosols, methane, land use and the Sun also matter; CO2 is the largest net contributor.
sequence: Ice cores: CO2 from about 180 ppm in ice ages to about 280 ppm in warm periods, over 800,000 years.
Forcing as a number: a log formula, and what doubling does.
Feedbacks: water vapour and ice-albedo amplify; clouds are the main uncertainty.
Fingerprints: the stratosphere cools while the surface warms; isotopes in CO2 point to fossil carbon.
Observed warming: 1.09 C (2011 to 2020 against 1850 to 1900, AR6).
examples: Doubling from 280 to 560 ppm: 5.35 x ln 2 = 3.7 W/m2. Reaching 420 ppm: 5.35 x ln 1.5 = 2.17 W/m2.
With sensitivity 3 degrees per doubling, 280 to 420 ppm gives 3 x log2(1.5) = 1.75 degrees at equilibrium.

figures.shows: Global temperature anomaly 1850 to now with natural-only and natural-plus-human model bands.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the model bands.

figures.shows: Forcing against CO2 concentration, log shape, with 280, 420, 560 marked.
figures.learnerAction: Move along the curve.

questionPlan.sample: Use forcing = 5.35 x ln(C / C0). What is the forcing for a doubling of CO2, in W/m2 to one decimal?
Climate sensitivity is 3 degrees C per doubling. How many degrees of equilibrium warming for CO2 rising from 280 to 1,120 ppm?
Why does each extra ppm of CO2 add less forcing than the one before?
questionPlan.answer: Absorption by the strongest bands is already near saturated, so the effect is logarithmic
choices: Absorption by the strongest bands is already near saturated, so the effect is logarithmic
Forcing is capped by the Sun

lessons.title: How ecosystems run
lessons.objective: Follow energy through food chains and predict a population limited by its environment.

concepts.title: Trophic efficiency
concepts.summary: Roughly 10 percent of the energy at one level reaches the next, so chains are short.

concepts.title: Carrying capacity
concepts.summary: The population an environment can sustain; logistic growth slows as N approaches K.

misconceptions: Energy cycles through ecosystems like matter. Matter cycles; energy flows through once and leaves as heat.
Removing a rare top predator changes little. A keystone species can have an outsized effect: Paine's 1966 starfish removal halved species richness in tide pools.
Populations grow without limit if they have food. Growth slows near carrying capacity.
sequence: Producers capture sunlight; consumers and decomposers use what they make.
Energy pyramid and the 10 percent rule.
Nutrient cycles close; energy does not.
Logistic growth with a stepping rule.
Connect to the carbon cycle: primary production is the biggest land-ocean carbon flux.
examples: 10,000 kJ in plants gives 1,000 in herbivores, 100 in carnivores, 10 in top carnivores.

figures.shows: Population against time: exponential versus logistic.
figures.learnerAction: Change r and K and watch the curve.

figures.shows: Energy pyramid with kJ values at each level.
figures.learnerAction: Hover a level to see what was lost as heat.

questionPlan.sample: Plants contain 50,000 kJ. Energy passes up 3 levels at 10 percent each. How many kJ reach the third consumer level?
N = 200, r = 0.4, K = 1,000. Use N_next = N + rN(1 - N/K). What is N_next?
What is the name for a species whose removal changes an ecosystem far more than its numbers suggest?

historyNotes: Robert Paine removed the starfish Pisaster ochraceus from tide pools on the coast of Washington State in 1966 and watched species richness fall.

lessons.title: Resources, limits and choices
lessons.objective: Work with stocks and flows, the energy units used for supply and the arithmetic of growing demand.

concepts.title: Stocks and flows
concepts.summary: A stock changes by inflow minus outflow; a stock falls when use exceeds renewal.

concepts.title: Capacity factor
concepts.summary: Actual energy produced divided by what the plant would produce at full power all year (8,760 hours).

misconceptions: Reserves divided by annual use is the time left. With demand growing, the time is shorter.
Power and energy are the same. Power is a rate in kW; energy is kW x hours in kWh.
Water is plentiful on a blue planet. About 2.5 percent is fresh, and most of that is ice or deep groundwater.
sequence: Fresh water: 97.5 percent of Earth's water is salt; of the fresh 2.5 percent, about 69 percent is ice.
Stocks and flows: a bathtub model of aquifers and soils.
Depletion arithmetic with and without growth.
Power, energy and capacity factor.
Weigh trade-offs for fuels, wind, solar and nuclear in land, emissions and reliability.
examples: Reserves 300, use 10 per year: static life 30 years. If use grows 5 percent per year, T = ln(1 + 0.05 x 300/10) / 0.05 = ln 2.5 / 0.05 = 18.3 years.
A 1 MW solar farm at a 25 percent capacity factor makes 8,760 x 0.25 = 2,190 MWh a year.

figures.shows: Reserves against time for flat use and for growing use.
figures.learnerAction: Change the growth rate.

figures.shows: Technologies with capacity factor, land use and emissions per kWh, as ranges.
figures.learnerAction: Sort by a column.

questionPlan.sample: Reserves are 300 units, use is 10 units a year and grows 5 percent a year. Using T = ln(1 + gR/P)/g, how many years last, to the nearest year?
A 3 MW wind farm has a capacity factor of 0.35. How many MWh does it produce in a year of 8,760 hours?
A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. How much energy does it use?

courseCheck: Mixed items: convert a plate rate to distance, half-life dating, pressure at altitude, absorbed solar power and effective temperature, cloud base, sea-level arithmetic, GtC to ppm, forcing for a CO2 change, energy loss up a food chain, and depletion time. Include classification of a boundary or rock and two reasoning questions about evidence for human-driven warming.
platformNeeds: A map figure (plates, hotspot tracks, ocean currents, climate zones) with layers and hover labels. Fallback: svg_figure with simplified outlines.
A cross-section figure type of Earth (to scale) with wave paths. Fallback: svg_figure.
An energy-budget explorer: sliders for albedo and greenhouse strength with a computed surface temperature. Fallback: graph_plot with fixed cases.
A real-data series loader for Mauna Loa CO2, global temperature and sea level (public NOAA, NASA, Copernicus data). Fallback: data_series with a decimated table written into the lesson.

URLs are standard locations as remembered; Physical Geology, 2nd edition (BCcampus) is believed to be CC BY 4.0 and is used instead of an OpenStax geology title, since OpenStax has none.
Layer depths and radii (2,891 km, 6,371 km, crust 7 and 35 km) from memory.
Mean ocean depth 3,700 m, ocean area 361 million km2 and 90 percent of excess heat in the ocean (AR6) are from memory.
Carbon-14 half-life 5,730 years, uranium-238 4.468 billion years, Earth age 4.54 billion years and Patterson 1953-56 dating are from memory.
Atmospheric carbon stock about 870 GtC, 2.13 GtC per ppm, airborne fraction about 45 percent, 280 ppm pre-industrial and above 420 ppm now are from memory; check the latest NOAA and GCP figures.
AR6 observed warming 1.09 C and equilibrium climate sensitivity best estimate 3 C (likely 2.5 to 4 C) are from memory; the forcing coefficient 5.35 is the Myhre et al. 1998 value.
Paine's 1966 starfish result ('halved richness') and Wegener dates (1912, 1915) are from memory.
The 125 m per degree cloud-base rule and the 10 percent trophic efficiency are rules of thumb, not exact.
Fresh-water shares (97.5 percent salt, about 69 percent of fresh water as ice) are from memory of the USGS figures.
